survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study pooled PIRLS 2006, 2011, and 2016 across 61 participating countries (total 786,041 students) and estimated the Rasch and Skip/IRTree models using senate weights. The authors followed PIRLS procedures for handling missing responses: not-reached items were treated as not administered for both item calibration and ability estimation, while skipped items were treated as not administered for item calibration but handled differently for ability estimation depending on the model (IAS vs Skip model). The analysis assumes measurement invariance and uses the pooled international sample rather than country-specific re-estimation for the main comparisons. The manuscript does not report replicate-weight methods (e.g., BRR/jackknife), so uncertainty estimation at replicate level cannot be confirmed from the provided text.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This paper does not use PV-based achievement scores as the dependent variable; instead, it compares psychometric missing-response treatments within an IRT/IRTree framework (skipped vs not-reached) and estimates latent traits and item difficulties under different missing-data strategies. Because the study’s core comparison is model-based treatment of missing responses (IAS vs Skip model) rather than an explicit PV-imputation workflow, the manuscript does not provide a standard missing-data handling label (e.g., listwise deletion or multiple imputation) for the student-item response matrix. Therefore, missing-data handling is not reported in the sense required by the schema, even though the missing-response mechanism is explicitly modeled.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PIRLS 2006, 2011, and 2016 cycles pooled across the 61 participating countries. The analysis focuses on the treatment of skipped items versus not-reached items within the PIRLS missing-response framework. The manuscript states that partial credit items were transformed into full credit items and that discrimination/guessing parameters were omitted by using a Rasch model for computational feasibility; these simplifications were applied to enable comparison between the Rasch reference model and the IRTree Skip model. For both models, not-reached items were treated as not administered for item calibration and ability estimation, while skipped items were treated as not administered for item calibration; the key difference is how skipped items are handled during ability estimation (PIRLS IAS vs IRTree Skip model).

main_findings.target_variable: Item difficulty correspondence (Rasch vs Skip model)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Item difficulty correspondence was reported as perfect (correlation r = 0.998 across all items; r = 0.998 for full credit items; r = 0.997 for non-guessing items; r = 0.997 for full credit non-guessing items).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIRLS 2006/2011/2016 pooled reading the study leveraged the treatment distinction between skipped and not-reached items to compare Rasch item difficulty estimates against the IRTree Skip model, finding that item difficulty correspondence was essentially perfect because both approaches treat skipped items as not administered during item calibration. This indicates that changing the missing-response model mainly affects student/ability estimation rather than item difficulty calibration in PIRLS under the authors’ modeling choices.

main_findings.target_variable: Student ability vs skipping propensity disentanglement
main_findings.performance_metrics: Average country correlations: Rasch ability & θ2 (ability) M=0.853 (2006), 0.863 (2011), 0.886 (2016); Rasch ability & θ1 (skipping propensity) M=0.415 (2006), 0.367 (2011), 0.406 (2016). Correlation between θ2 and θ1: M=0.104 (2006), 0.113 (2011), 0.146 (2016). Correlations between % skipped and Rasch ability: −0.411 (2006), −0.372 (2011), −0.398 (2016); % skipped and θ2: −0.144 (2006), −0.151 (2011), −0.179 (2016); % skipped and θ1: −0.935 (2006), −0.933 (2011), −0.912 (2016).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIRLS 2006/2011/2016 pooled reading the study leveraged the skipped-item missing-response treatment to predict student ability estimates and separate them from skipping propensity (θ1) via the IRTree Skip model, finding that the IRTree approach reduced the correlation between ability and the proportion of skipped items compared with the Rasch model. This indicates that adopting an IRTree-style missing-response model could yield more valid reading literacy estimates by accounting for students’ propensity to skip, which may improve the fairness of country comparisons when skipping is non-negligible.

main_findings.target_variable: Country mean scores and rankings (Rasch vs Skip model)
main_findings.performance_metrics: The study reported an almost perfect relationship between country mean scores and country rankings across models (Fig. 5). It also reported that differences are not important for the pooled sample overall, but can appear within countries across cycles, exemplified by Morocco and Kuwait showing model-dependent mean differences when skipped-item proportions are high.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIRLS 2006/2011/2016 pooled reading the study leveraged the skipped-item missing-response treatment to predict country mean scores and rankings under Rasch versus the IRTree Skip model, finding that aggregated scores showed no important differences for the pooled sample but some differences within countries across cycles when skipped-item proportions were high. This indicates that PIRLS reporting may be robust at the league-table level overall, yet country-specific policy interpretations could change when skipping patterns vary across cycles.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes PIRLS reading data from the 2006, 2011, and 2016 cycles pooled across 61 countries (N=786,041 students) to evaluate how treating skipped and not-reached items affects estimated item difficulty, student ability, and country scores. The authors compare an IRTree Skip model (a multidimensional IRT framework that jointly estimates ability and skipping propensity) against a Rasch reference model using PIRLS’s standard missing-response handling (skipped items treated as incorrect for ability estimation; not-reached items treated as not administered). At the item level, correspondence between Rasch and IRTree item difficulties was essentially perfect (e.g., r≈0.998). At the student level, the IRTree model disentangled ability (θ2) from skipping propensity (θ1), reducing the association between ability and skipped-item proportions (e.g., correlations of % skipped with Rasch ability around −0.41 vs with θ2 around −0.14 to −0.18). At the country level, overall rankings were almost unchanged, but within-country differences across cycles emerged for countries with higher skipping rates (e.g., Morocco and Kuwait).
data.null_fields_interpretation: The paper is an IRT/IRTree psychometric modeling study rather than an ML predictive-modeling study: it does not train supervised ML algorithms, and therefore ml_techniques is intentionally empty. As a result, the schema’s ML-specific fields (primary/all_techniques) are not applicable, while the substantive findings come from comparing latent-trait measurement models under different missing-response treatments.
